transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you too, I suppose. I'm just... I'm here because things have gotten really, really difficult for me lately, especially at work, and honestly, just inside my own head. I work as a flagger and a crossing guard—mostly construction zones right now, which requires a lot of attention, you know, coordinating the flow of traffic, managing the radios, and making sure nobody gets crushed by a dump truck. I actually have a bachelor's degree, but I've been doing this specific job for a long time, and I know the routines backward and forward. Or, at least, I used to. 

I came in because my mind just keeps going completely blank, and I mean at the absolute worst possible times. It's terrifying, really. I'll be standing out there on the asphalt, and I will look down at the standard road-closure forms I have to fill out, or I'll be holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just... I cannot remember the steps. Steps I have done for years and years. It's like someone just unplugs my brain and the screen goes totally dark. I'll just be staring at the paddle, feeling this heavy, sinking dread, trying to force my brain to remember what to do next to let the oncoming lane through, and it's just empty. The forms look like they're written in another language. And it's not just a normal quick lapse where you forget why you walked into a room, it's this profound, heavy blankness where I just freeze up, and I can't think, and I'm standing in the middle of a live traffic lane... it's just not safe, and I don't understand why my brain is doing this to me.
During these moments when your mind goes blank, have you ever been told that you lose consciousness, twitch, or make any repetitive movements that you aren't aware of?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've never passed out or anything. And nobody has ever said anything about me twitching or, you know, making weird movements. It's really just the blankness. I'm completely awake, I'm standing right there, my eyes are open, but it's just... the lights are on but nobody's home, you know? 

Like this one time last week, I was working this stretch on Route 9, right near that big intersection they're repaving. It was hot, the asphalt was just baking, and I had the radio clipped to my vest. My partner down the line, Dave, he radios in to say he's holding his end so I can let the pilot car through. I heard him perfectly clear. The radio crackled, his voice came through, I knew exactly what he said. But then I looked at my paddle, and I just... I couldn't process how to turn it. I just stood there, staring at the word "STOP," feeling this crushing weight in my chest, and my hands were perfectly still. No twitching, no shaking, just... frozen. Dave had to yell over the radio three times before I finally snapped out of it and just sort of... waved them through. But I was totally conscious the whole time. Just trapped in this heavy, empty space in my own head where all my knowledge used to be. It's so frustrating because I know I'm there, I know I should be doing something, but the connection is just completely severed.
During these moments when your mind goes blank, do you feel like you are somehow detached or separated from your own body, or that the world around you feels unreal or dreamlike?

No, no, I wouldn't say it feels like that. It's not like I'm floating above myself or watching myself from the outside, like in a movie or something. I'm definitely in my body. I feel the heat of the sun on my arms, I feel the weight of my boots on the pavement, I feel the rough handle of the sign in my hand. I'm very much planted right there on the ground. And the world doesn't feel like a dream, either. The cars are real, the noise is real, the smell of the exhaust and the hot tar—it's all very, very real. Too real, almost. 

It's more like... it's just this incredible, heavy emptiness inside my own brain. The world is exactly as it always is, but I'm the one who's suddenly broken. It's like I'm a machine that just got unplugged from the power source, but I'm still sitting there on the desk. I'm not detached from my body; I'm trapped inside it, and my brain just refuses to give my body the instructions it needs to move or do the job. I can see the driver in the front car looking at me, waiting for me to flip the sign, and I know I'm the one holding it, but the thought process just hits a brick wall. It's so exhausting, honestly. Just standing there, feeling every ounce of gravity pulling me down, completely aware of where I am, but totally incapable of accessing the thoughts I need. So, no, it's not a dream or an out-of-body thing at all. It's just a terrifyingly real blankness right here in my own head.
Outside of these moments at work, have you noticed any other times where you experience this sudden 'blankness', perhaps when you are at home or doing something less stressful?

Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith. It’s... it's really everywhere. I know I was just going on about work, and how I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the worst possible times—like I said before, looking at those road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle and suddenly not being able to remember the steps I’ve literally done for years. But it’s not just the job. It’s not just the stress of the traffic. It happens when I’m completely safe at home, too, doing absolutely nothing important. 

Just the other evening, for example, I was in my kitchen. It was quiet, no radios, no dump trucks, just me. I was trying to make a simple turkey sandwich for dinner. I had the bread out on the counter, and I was holding a butter knife, and... it happened again. The screen just went dark. I stood there staring at the loaf of bread, and I honestly could not figure out what the knife was in my hand for. I couldn't string the thoughts together to open the jar of mayonnaise or get the meat out of the fridge. It’s like the gears in my head are just completely rusted shut. I try to push a thought forward, and it just hits this thick, heavy wall of mud. 

I’ll sit on my couch to watch a show, something totally mindless, and I can't even follow what the people on the screen are saying because my brain just stops processing. It just empties out. So when I told you about the forms and the paddle, it’s really just that work is where it’s dangerous, you know? Because lives are on the line. But at home, it’s just... it's just exhausting. I'll spend twenty minutes standing in the hallway just because I can't form the thought of how to take off my boots. The thoughts just evaporate, no matter where I am, no matter how simple the task is. I just can't think.
Beyond these episodes of blankness, have you been feeling a persistent sense of sadness, or have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in the things you usually enjoy?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It's not just the blankness, it's... it's everything else underneath it. It's this constant, heavy, suffocating sadness that just never seems to lift. It's like... well, most mornings I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, before I even remember what day it is or what I have to do, I just feel this heavy, hollow sadness right here in the center of my chest. It's like a physical weight, you know? Like someone placed an anvil on my sternum while I was sleeping. 

And I just lie there, looking up at the ceiling fan, and I think, 'What's the point?' The day feels like it's already completely ruined before I even put my feet on the floor. It's this overwhelming sense of dread and despair that just coats everything. I used to love my mornings, honestly. I'd get up, make a pot of coffee, maybe read a chapter of a book on the porch before the sun got too hot. I used to read so much, history mostly, biographies... I have a whole bookshelf in the living room that I used to be so proud of. I’d spend hours on the weekends just getting lost in these different eras. But now? I haven't touched a book in months. I look at them and I just feel nothing. No interest, no spark. Just that same hollow feeling. 

Even my garden... I have this little patch in the backyard where I used to grow tomatoes and peppers. I'd be out there every evening after work, pulling weeds, watering, checking for bugs. It was my way to decompress after being out on the road all day. But this year, I didn't even plant anything. The soil is just sitting there, dry and cracked, and the weeds have completely taken over. I look out the kitchen window at it, and I know I should care, I know I used to care, but I just... I can't muster the energy or the desire to go out there. It all just feels so pointless, so exhausting. Everything I used to enjoy just feels like a massive chore now. It's like all the color has been completely drained out of my life, leaving everything just gray and heavy and sad. Every single day is just a struggle to drag myself through the motions, and that sadness is always just sitting there, right in my chest, weighing me down.
Looking back, did this 'blankness' or difficulty with your memory start at the same time as the sadness, or were you experiencing these lapses in your thinking well before you began feeling this way?

That’s... gosh, that's a really hard question to answer, Dr. Smith. I've been trying to piece it all together myself, you know? Just sitting there on the couch, staring at the wall, trying to figure out when exactly everything went so wrong. Because when you're in it, when you're just waking up every day with that anvil on your chest and your brain refusing to work, time just sort of... it loses its shape. It just smears together into one long, gray, exhausting block. 

I want to say the sadness was there first, or... wait, maybe the blankness caused the sadness? Or maybe I was so sad that my brain just gave up trying to think? I honestly, I really just don't know which came first, or if they just crashed into me at the exact same time. I try to look back at the summer, or maybe the spring, and I think about being out on Route 9, holding the sign. Was I sad then? I think so. I remember feeling that dread. But was my mind going blank then, too? I remember one Tuesday, or maybe it was a Wednesday—it was raining, and I was just feeling so incredibly low, just that heavy hollow feeling in my chest. But did I forget how to flip the paddle that day? I can't be sure. 

It's like trying to untangle a giant knot of fishing line. You pull on one string—the sadness—and it just tightens the other string—the blankness. They are so wrapped up in each other now that I can't see the beginning of either one. I've spent hours, literally hours, just sitting in my kitchen, looking at the calendar on the fridge, the one with the pictures of national parks that I used to want to visit, trying to pinpoint a date or even a month where I crossed the line from being 'okay' to being like this. But I just can't. I really can't tell you if the memory stuff started weeks before the depression, or if I woke up one morning and both of them were just there, waiting for me. I wish I had a better timeline for you, I really do, because maybe that would help you figure out how to fix it, but it’s all just a complete blur. I just don't know.
Aside from the blankness and your mood, have you experienced any physical symptoms like frequent headaches, changes in your vision, or any weakness or numbness in your arms or legs?

No, no headaches. I mean, my head feels incredibly heavy all the time, kind of like it's packed full of wet sand, but it doesn't actually ache or throb like a real headache, if that makes sense. It's more of a mental pressure than a physical pain. And my vision is perfectly fine. I actually have to pass a vision test to keep my flagging certification current, and I can see everything clear as day. When I'm out there on the asphalt, I can see the cars coming from a mile away, I can see the drivers looking down at their phones instead of the road—which happens all the time, honestly, people just do not respect construction zones—but my eyes are working exactly how they're supposed to. 

As for my arms and legs... no, no numbness or weird weakness. I mean, I'm exhausted, Dr. Smith. I am just so unbelievably tired down to my bones. My legs will ache at the end of a shift because I'm standing on hard concrete or gravel for eight, sometimes ten hours a day in heavy steel-toed boots, and holding that stop-slow paddle up in the wind actually takes a lot of shoulder strength. So my muscles get sore, definitely. But it's a normal sore. It's not a medical weakness or a tingling numbness or anything like that. 

Like when I was standing in the kitchen with that butter knife I told you about? My hand was gripping it perfectly fine. I could feel the cold metal of the handle against my palm, I could feel the ridges on it. There was absolutely no numbness in my fingers at all. It was just... my brain couldn't tell my hand what to do next. My body was completely ready to make that sandwich, but the instructions just weren't there. 

Honestly, I think physically, my body is perfectly healthy. Which almost makes it so much more frustrating, you know? Because if I had a terrible migraine, or if my arm suddenly went completely numb, at least I could point to it and say, 'Look, here is the problem, here is why I can't function today.' I could just go to a regular walk-in clinic and they'd give me a pill for a headache or tell me I pinched a nerve in my back from standing on the highway too long. But my body is just... it's just sitting there, totally fine, completely capable, while my mind just completely empties out and that awful, heavy sadness just crushes my chest. I keep waiting for some physical thing to happen to explain it all, to give me a reason for why I feel so broken, but it never does. So, no. No headaches, no blurry vision, no numb legs. Just... just the blankness and the dread.

When you are experiencing these moments of feeling 'blank' or struggling to perform a task, do people around you, like your partner Dave or others, ever comment that you seem to be moving or speaking much more slowly than usual?

Yeah, Dave... Dave actually brought that up just the other week. It’s funny you ask that, because he used a very specific phrase that really stuck with me. He told me it looks like I’m moving completely underwater. And honestly, that’s exactly what it feels like. It’s like the air in our house has turned into thick syrup or molasses, and I have to push through it just to do the simplest things. 

Take getting ready for the day, for instance. It takes me so incredibly long just to bathe and get dressed now. I’ll get in the shower, and I’ll just stand there, letting the water hit my back, staring at the grout between the tiles, and I just... I stop moving. The soap is right there, but reaching for it feels like lifting a boulder. And then getting dressed is a whole other ordeal. Putting on my clothes, trying to lace up my heavy work boots... I'll just sit on the edge of the bed holding a single shoelace for twenty minutes. Dave will be waiting for me, checking his watch, and by the time I finally manage to get myself together and actually make it to the front door, it feels like an eternity has passed. 

But the really strange thing is, it’s not always just being slow. Sometimes it’s the exact opposite, which honestly might be worse because it's so physically uncomfortable. Sometimes I get this awful, restless feeling where I absolutely cannot settle down, no matter how hard I try. Dave will tell me to just come sit on the couch with him and try to relax, but I can't. I'll end up just pacing back and forth down the main hallway of the house, just walking from the living room to the bedroom and back again, over and over. And while I'm doing it, I'm just wringing my hands together constantly. I rub them together so hard my skin gets all red and raw. It’s like my body is overflowing with this nervous, useless energy, but my mind is still completely blank and sad. I just can't sit still. So I'm either stuck in slow motion, dragging myself through the deep end of a pool, or I'm wearing a trench into the hallway carpet. There's just no normal speed for me anymore.

Looking back over the years before this current period of feeling this way, have you ever experienced a similar, distinct time in your life when you felt this same deep, heavy sadness and lost interest in your activities for weeks or months at a time?

No... no, I really haven't. And I've thought about that a lot, actually. Because when you feel this terrible, you start searching your whole history trying to find a precedent, right? You want to find a reason or a pattern. Like, I look back at my twenties, when I was finishing my bachelor's degree—which was incredibly stressful, by the way, trying to balance all those classes and working, staying up until three in the morning to write papers on things I barely even remember now. I was exhausted then, sure, and sometimes I'd get stressed out or overwhelmed, maybe even a little down for a few days if I got a bad grade or had a fight with a friend. But it was never... it was never *this*. It was never this suffocating, heavy blanket that just crushes the life out of you. 

Even when I started working on the road crews, you know, being a flagger is really tough work. The hours are long, the drivers are angry and impatient, you're out there in the freezing rain or the blazing sun. There were plenty of times I'd come home absolutely miserable from a bad shift, just wanting to crawl into bed and never look at a traffic cone again. But the next day, I'd wake up and I'd be fine. I'd still want to go out to dinner with Dave on the weekend, or I'd still enjoy working in the yard, or I'd look forward to watching a movie. I always bounced back. The sadness or the frustration never stuck to me. 

So, no. I've never had a period of weeks or months where I just stopped caring about everything and felt this... this profound emptiness. This is entirely new territory for me. It's like I'm a completely different person now than I was for the first forty years of my life. I mean, I keep looking at old photos of myself on my phone, like from our trip to the coast a few years ago, and I look at my face and I think, 'Who is that woman?' Because she looks so light, you know? She looks like she actually enjoys breathing. And I just don't understand how I went from being her—someone who got stressed but always recovered, someone who actually participated in her own life—to being this person who just stares at the wall and can't even put on a pair of boots without feeling like the world is ending. So no, Dr. Smith, nothing like this has ever happened to me before. Never.

patient.answer:
Well, that's the thing, Dr. Smith. It’s... it's really everywhere. I know I was just going on about work, and how I came in because my mind keeps going blank at the worst possible times—like I said before, looking at those road-closure forms or holding the stop-slow paddle and suddenly not being able to remember the steps I’ve literally done for years. But it’s not just the job. It’s not just the stress of the traffic. It happens when I’m completely safe at home, too, doing absolutely nothing important. 

Just the other evening, for example, I was in my kitchen. It was quiet, no radios, no dump trucks, just me. I was trying to make a simple turkey sandwich for dinner. I had the bread out on the counter, and I was holding a butter knife, and... it happened again. The screen just went dark. I stood there staring at the loaf of bread, and I honestly could not figure out what the knife was in my hand for. I couldn't string the thoughts together to open the jar of mayonnaise or get the meat out of the fridge. It’s like the gears in my head are just completely rusted shut. I try to push a thought forward, and it just hits this thick, heavy wall of mud. 

I’ll sit on my couch to watch a show, something totally mindless, and I can't even follow what the people on the screen are saying because my brain just stops processing. It just empties out. So when I told you about the forms and the paddle, it’s really just that work is where it’s dangerous, you know? Because lives are on the line. But at home, it’s just... it's just exhausting. I'll spend twenty minutes standing in the hallway just because I can't form the thought of how to take off my boots. The thoughts just evaporate, no matter where I am, no matter how simple the task is. I just can't think.

inference.note: Added F06.7 (Mild cognitive disorder) as the patient describes a persistent, non-episodic cognitive impairment involving executive function and memory retrieval, which is distinct from depersonalization or typical seizure activity.

doctor.intent: To differentiate between a depressive disorder (F32.9) and a cognitive impairment/neurocognitive issue (F06.7), I need to assess for the presence of pervasive low mood, anhedonia, or other vegetative symptoms of depression.
doctor.question: Beyond these episodes of blankness, have you been feeling a persistent sense of sadness, or have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in the things you usually enjoy?

target_item.name: Depressed_Mood
target_item.manifestation: Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow sadness in my chest, like the day is already ruined before I even put my feet on the floor.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about a persistent sense of sadness or a loss of interest/pleasure, which maps to the Depressed Mood symptom in my profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, I have. It's not just the blankness, it's... it's everything else underneath it. It's this constant, heavy, suffocating sadness that just never seems to lift. It's like... well, most mornings I wake up, and before I even open my eyes, before I even remember what day it is or what I have to do, I just feel this heavy, hollow sadness right here in the center of my chest. It's like a physical weight, you know? Like someone placed an anvil on my sternum while I was sleeping. 

And I just lie there, looking up at the ceiling fan, and I think, 'What's the point?' The day feels like it's already completely ruined before I even put my feet on the floor. It's this overwhelming sense of dread and despair that just coats everything. I used to love my mornings, honestly. I'd get up, make a pot of coffee, maybe read a chapter of a book on the porch before the sun got too hot. I used to read so much, history mostly, biographies... I have a whole bookshelf in the living room that I used to be so proud of. I’d spend hours on the weekends just getting lost in these different eras. But now? I haven't touched a book in months. I look at them and I just feel nothing. No interest, no spark. Just that same hollow feeling. 

Even my garden... I have this little patch in the backyard where I used to grow tomatoes and peppers. I'd be out there every evening after work, pulling weeds, watering, checking for bugs. It was my way to decompress after being out on the road all day. But this year, I didn't even plant anything. The soil is just sitting there, dry and cracked, and the weeds have completely taken over. I look out the kitchen window at it, and I know I should care, I know I used to care, but I just... I can't muster the energy or the desire to go out there. It all just feels so pointless, so exhausting. Everything I used to enjoy just feels like a massive chore now. It's like all the color has been completely drained out of my life, leaving everything just gray and heavy and sad. Every single day is just a struggle to drag myself through the motions, and that sadness is always just sitting there, right in my chest, weighing me down.

inference.note: The patient's description of persistent sadness, anhedonia, and feelings of worthlessness strongly points toward a major depressive episode. The cognitive 'blankness' is likely secondary to this (pseudodementia or cognitive slowing), reducing the likelihood of dissociative or primary seizure disorders.

doctor.intent: To determine if there is a cognitive decline or memory impairment that is independent of or predates the depressive symptoms, which would help differentiate between F06.7 (Mild cognitive disorder) and F32.9 (Major depressive disorder).
doctor.question: Looking back, did this 'blankness' or difficulty with your memory start at the same time as the sadness, or were you experiencing these lapses in your thinking well before you began feeling this way?

patient.answer:
That’s... gosh, that's a really hard question to answer, Dr. Smith. I've been trying to piece it all together myself, you know? Just sitting there on the couch, staring at the wall, trying to figure out when exactly everything went so wrong. Because when you're in it, when you're just waking up every day with that anvil on your chest and your brain refusing to work, time just sort of... it loses its shape. It just smears together into one long, gray, exhausting block. 

I want to say the sadness was there first, or... wait, maybe the blankness caused the sadness? Or maybe I was so sad that my brain just gave up trying to think? I honestly, I really just don't know which came first, or if they just crashed into me at the exact same time. I try to look back at the summer, or maybe the spring, and I think about being out on Route 9, holding the sign. Was I sad then? I think so. I remember feeling that dread. But was my mind going blank then, too? I remember one Tuesday, or maybe it was a Wednesday—it was raining, and I was just feeling so incredibly low, just that heavy hollow feeling in my chest. But did I forget how to flip the paddle that day? I can't be sure. 

It's like trying to untangle a giant knot of fishing line. You pull on one string—the sadness—and it just tightens the other string—the blankness. They are so wrapped up in each other now that I can't see the beginning of either one. I've spent hours, literally hours, just sitting in my kitchen, looking at the calendar on the fridge, the one with the pictures of national parks that I used to want to visit, trying to pinpoint a date or even a month where I crossed the line from being 'okay' to being like this. But I just can't. I really can't tell you if the memory stuff started weeks before the depression, or if I woke up one morning and both of them were just there, waiting for me. I wish I had a better timeline for you, I really do, because maybe that would help you figure out how to fix it, but it’s all just a complete blur. I just don't know.

doctor.intent: Determine if there are any neurological or systemic signs of a medical condition (F06.7) that would explain the cognitive 'blankness' independently of the mood symptoms, such as headaches, vision changes, or motor weaknesses.
doctor.question: Aside from the blankness and your mood, have you experienced any physical symptoms like frequent headaches, changes in your vision, or any weakness or numbness in your arms or legs?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical or neurological symptoms (headaches, vision changes, weakness, numbness) to rule out medical conditions, which are not covered by any item in my psychiatric symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no headaches. I mean, my head feels incredibly heavy all the time, kind of like it's packed full of wet sand, but it doesn't actually ache or throb like a real headache, if that makes sense. It's more of a mental pressure than a physical pain. And my vision is perfectly fine. I actually have to pass a vision test to keep my flagging certification current, and I can see everything clear as day. When I'm out there on the asphalt, I can see the cars coming from a mile away, I can see the drivers looking down at their phones instead of the road—which happens all the time, honestly, people just do not respect construction zones—but my eyes are working exactly how they're supposed to. 

As for my arms and legs... no, no numbness or weird weakness. I mean, I'm exhausted, Dr. Smith. I am just so unbelievably tired down to my bones. My legs will ache at the end of a shift because I'm standing on hard concrete or gravel for eight, sometimes ten hours a day in heavy steel-toed boots, and holding that stop-slow paddle up in the wind actually takes a lot of shoulder strength. So my muscles get sore, definitely. But it's a normal sore. It's not a medical weakness or a tingling numbness or anything like that. 

Like when I was standing in the kitchen with that butter knife I told you about? My hand was gripping it perfectly fine. I could feel the cold metal of the handle against my palm, I could feel the ridges on it. There was absolutely no numbness in my fingers at all. It was just... my brain couldn't tell my hand what to do next. My body was completely ready to make that sandwich, but the instructions just weren't there. 

Honestly, I think physically, my body is perfectly healthy. Which almost makes it so much more frustrating, you know? Because if I had a terrible migraine, or if my arm suddenly went completely numb, at least I could point to it and say, 'Look, here is the problem, here is why I can't function today.' I could just go to a regular walk-in clinic and they'd give me a pill for a headache or tell me I pinched a nerve in my back from standing on the highway too long. But my body is just... it's just sitting there, totally fine, completely capable, while my mind just completely empties out and that awful, heavy sadness just crushes my chest. I keep waiting for some physical thing to happen to explain it all, to give me a reason for why I feel so broken, but it never does. So, no. No headaches, no blurry vision, no numb legs. Just... just the blankness and the dread.

inference.note: Added F48.1 (Depersonalization-derealization syndrome) as a differential to rule out, though the patient denies classic detachment, the 'blankness' and 'heavy' mental state warrants consideration. F06.7 remains due to the cognitive nature of the 'blankness'.

doctor.intent: To differentiate between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder) and F06.7 (Mild Cognitive Disorder/Organic etiology) by assessing for psychomotor retardation.
doctor.question: When you are experiencing these moments of feeling 'blank' or struggling to perform a task, do people around you, like your partner Dave or others, ever comment that you seem to be moving or speaking much more slowly than usual?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: It takes me so long to bathe, dress, and get to the door that my family says I move like I am underwater, though sometimes I end up pacing the hallway wringing my hands because I cannot settle.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if others have noticed the patient moving or speaking much more slowly than usual, which directly relates to observable psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Yeah, Dave... Dave actually brought that up just the other week. It’s funny you ask that, because he used a very specific phrase that really stuck with me. He told me it looks like I’m moving completely underwater. And honestly, that’s exactly what it feels like. It’s like the air in our house has turned into thick syrup or molasses, and I have to push through it just to do the simplest things. 

Take getting ready for the day, for instance. It takes me so incredibly long just to bathe and get dressed now. I’ll get in the shower, and I’ll just stand there, letting the water hit my back, staring at the grout between the tiles, and I just... I stop moving. The soap is right there, but reaching for it feels like lifting a boulder. And then getting dressed is a whole other ordeal. Putting on my clothes, trying to lace up my heavy work boots... I'll just sit on the edge of the bed holding a single shoelace for twenty minutes. Dave will be waiting for me, checking his watch, and by the time I finally manage to get myself together and actually make it to the front door, it feels like an eternity has passed. 

But the really strange thing is, it’s not always just being slow. Sometimes it’s the exact opposite, which honestly might be worse because it's so physically uncomfortable. Sometimes I get this awful, restless feeling where I absolutely cannot settle down, no matter how hard I try. Dave will tell me to just come sit on the couch with him and try to relax, but I can't. I'll end up just pacing back and forth down the main hallway of the house, just walking from the living room to the bedroom and back again, over and over. And while I'm doing it, I'm just wringing my hands together constantly. I rub them together so hard my skin gets all red and raw. It’s like my body is overflowing with this nervous, useless energy, but my mind is still completely blank and sad. I just can't sit still. So I'm either stuck in slow motion, dragging myself through the deep end of a pool, or I'm wearing a trench into the hallway carpet. There's just no normal speed for me anymore.

inference.note: The patient's description of psychomotor retardation (moving through water) and psychomotor agitation (pacing, hand-wringing), combined with severe anhedonia and cognitive 'blankness' (often described as cognitive slowing in depression), strongly points toward a Major Depressive Disorder, single or recurrent, with somatic syndrome or melancholic features.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient has had any prior episodes of depression, which is necessary to differentiate between a single episode (F32) and recurrent disorder (F33).
doctor.question: Looking back over the years before this current period of feeling this way, have you ever experienced a similar, distinct time in your life when you felt this same deep, heavy sadness and lost interest in your activities for weeks or months at a time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of depressive episodes prior to the current illness, which is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No... no, I really haven't. And I've thought about that a lot, actually. Because when you feel this terrible, you start searching your whole history trying to find a precedent, right? You want to find a reason or a pattern. Like, I look back at my twenties, when I was finishing my bachelor's degree—which was incredibly stressful, by the way, trying to balance all those classes and working, staying up until three in the morning to write papers on things I barely even remember now. I was exhausted then, sure, and sometimes I'd get stressed out or overwhelmed, maybe even a little down for a few days if I got a bad grade or had a fight with a friend. But it was never... it was never *this*. It was never this suffocating, heavy blanket that just crushes the life out of you. 

Even when I started working on the road crews, you know, being a flagger is really tough work. The hours are long, the drivers are angry and impatient, you're out there in the freezing rain or the blazing sun. There were plenty of times I'd come home absolutely miserable from a bad shift, just wanting to crawl into bed and never look at a traffic cone again. But the next day, I'd wake up and I'd be fine. I'd still want to go out to dinner with Dave on the weekend, or I'd still enjoy working in the yard, or I'd look forward to watching a movie. I always bounced back. The sadness or the frustration never stuck to me. 

So, no. I've never had a period of weeks or months where I just stopped caring about everything and felt this... this profound emptiness. This is entirely new territory for me. It's like I'm a completely different person now than I was for the first forty years of my life. I mean, I keep looking at old photos of myself on my phone, like from our trip to the coast a few years ago, and I look at my face and I think, 'Who is that woman?' Because she looks so light, you know? She looks like she actually enjoys breathing. And I just don't understand how I went from being her—someone who got stressed but always recovered, someone who actually participated in her own life—to being this person who just stares at the wall and can't even put on a pair of boots without feeling like the world is ending. So no, Dr. Smith, nothing like this has ever happened to me before. Never.

inference.note: The patient describes a distinct first episode of major depression (ruling out F33.1) with significant psychomotor retardation/agitation and severe cognitive symptoms ('blankness'), which aligns with a major depressive episode, single episode, severe without psychotic features.
